title: Dense Event Ordering with a Multi-Pass Architecture
research_question: How should temporal-ordering systems and evaluation change when they must label densely connected event graphs rather than only a sparse set of preselected event pairs?
methodology: The paper introduces TimeBank-Dense, which densely annotates local temporal relations among events, time expressions, and document creation time, and uses it to evaluate a multi-pass system called CAEVO. CAEVO is a precision-ranked cascade of twelve rule-based and machine-learned sieves, with each sieve receiving the graph produced by earlier sieves. Transitive closure is applied after successive passes so earlier high-precision decisions constrain later decisions and infer additional edges. The system is compared with retrained TempEval-3 systems and is analyzed through component, edge-type, and relation-type ablations.

key_findings.finding: TimeBank-Dense contains 12,715 labeled temporal relations over 36 TimeBank newspaper articles and produces strongly connected local event-time graphs by requiring annotation of all relevant pairs within the same or neighboring sentences plus document-time links.
CAEVO achieves 50.7 F1 on the dense test setting, a 14% relative improvement over the retrained top TempEval-3 systems used for comparison.

Global transitive inference is a major contributor: adding transitivity raises the ablated CAEVO configuration from 32.1 to 39.8 F1, and the authors estimate that transitive inference alone contributes about ten percent performance improvement.
Edges produced through transitive inference have higher precision than edges directly classified by sieves, approximately 54.4-54.5% versus 49.8%.

Time-time relations constitute only 2.6% of the evaluated edges, yet removing the time-time sieve reduces overall performance by almost five percent because those relations affect other decisions through transitive closure.
Dense annotation reveals substantial uncertainty: VAGUE constitutes 46% of the annotated graph and can arise from genuine vagueness or annotator disagreement.

limitations: TimeBank-Dense covers only 36 newspaper articles, so the empirical setting is small and domain-specific.
The graph is locally dense rather than fully complete: explicit relations spanning two or more sentence boundaries are not annotated.
The relation inventory deliberately collapses finer Allen-style distinctions to improve annotation reliability.
VAGUE remains semantically ambiguous because it may indicate that no specific relation can be established or that several relations remain possible.
Annotator agreement is imperfect, with average pairwise precision of 65.1% and kappa values from 0.56 to 0.64.
The ordering experiments use gold event attributes for controlled analysis, and the temporal relation labels do not encode factuality or workflow states such as planned, canceled, or completed.
raw_claims: TimeBank-Dense was created to reduce the missing-relation ambiguity present in sparse temporal corpora.
The corpus labels temporal pairs within the same sentence and across immediately neighboring sentences.
The corpus contains 12,715 labeled relations across 36 newspaper documents.
Its relation inventory consists of BEFORE, AFTER, INCLUDES, IS_INCLUDED, SIMULTANEOUS, and VAGUE.
VAGUE accounts for 46% of the annotated temporal graph.
CAEVO processes temporal decisions through a precision-ordered sequence of twelve sieves.
Transitive closure is applied so that earlier temporal decisions constrain later ones.
CAEVO obtains 50.7 F1 in the dense evaluation.
The reported improvement over retrained TempEval-3 comparison systems is 14% relative F1.
Transitivity-derived edges are more precise than directly classified sieve edges.
Removing the time-time sieve materially harms global performance despite the small number of time-time edges.
CAEVO code and the TimeBank-Dense corpus were made publicly available.
